case_study_insert.main_stem: Tarnfield Blockworks (TBK) is a private limited company in the construction materials sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2011 by Priya Tarnfield, it makes precast concrete blocks for housebuilders and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TBK plans to invest $560,000 in an automated block-moulding line using recycled aggregate, financed by a $200,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 from a new share issue. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 55,000 units a year. TBK faces a defect rate of 3.4% in finished blocks and rising labour turnover among mould operators, which Priya wants solved before the new line starts.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: The moulding line produced 13,750 blocks last quarter with a defect rate of 3.4%, down from 4.9% a year earlier but still above the 1.5% target. Customer complaints about chipped blocks rose from 16 to 31 per month. Average order turnaround is 3.6 days. Trial use of recycled aggregate cut raw-material waste by 2.8% but raised mixing time by 1.2 minutes per batch. A survey of 250 housebuilders found that 61% would pay up to $0.30 more for lower-carbon blocks and 44% check a supplier's recycled content when tendering. A skills audit shows 14 of 48 operators lack training on the automated moulds; certified courses at the local college cost $640 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Tarnfield Blockworks for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate debt including TBK's $200,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.20 to $12.96 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills in manufacturing. (3) Cement, steel and recycled-aggregate input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while housing starts grew 4.0% and regional construction output expanded 3.6%.

questions.question_text: TBK plans to fund part of its $560,000 moulding-line expansion with a $200,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TBK of financing the expansion with $360,000 from a new share issue instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $360,000 share issue brings in equity that carries no interest and no fixed repayment dates, so TBK avoids loading a larger bank loan onto the $200,000 it already plans to borrow. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year and a 3.4% defect rate to fix, preserving cash flow matters: money not spent on loan interest can fund quality checks on the new automated moulds without raising the $15.00 selling price for housebuilders.

Point 2: New equity strengthens TBK's balance sheet and gives a larger capital base to absorb the risk of the $560,000 moulding line, which is why the board chose it over extra debt. Unlike a bigger loan, shares cannot be called in if the 3.4% defect rate persists and cash generation slips, so the business is less exposed to repossession. The trade-off is that Priya's existing ownership is diluted, but for a young 48-employee firm the reduced financial risk supports the lower-carbon positioning that 61% of surveyed builders value.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over a larger loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TBK's expansion, existing loan and housebuilder survey.

questions.question_text: TBK is launching lower-carbon recycled blocks. Consider trade-journal advertising, sponsorship of a local builders' association, or direct meetings with housebuilders. Which should TBK choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade-journal advertising: Placing adverts in housebuilding and construction journals would reach the 250 surveyed builders and many specifiers nationwide, supporting a premium lower-carbon image. It is credible and long-lived. Yet national print is expensive for a 48-employee company funding a $560,000 line, and much of the circulation lies beyond TBK's regional delivery area, so a large share of the spend cannot be converted into sales of 55,000 blocks.

Local builders' association sponsorship: Sponsoring a regional association is relatively cheap, builds goodwill and repeatedly exposes TBK to local small builders who make frequent repeat purchases. It suits a regional manufacturer. However, it cannot explain technical details such as the 2.8% waste reduction or the 1.5% defect target, and it will not reach the 44% of builders who check recycled content only when formally tendering.

Direct meetings with housebuilders: Priya's team can meet the largest regional housebuilders, present test data showing progress from 4.9% to a 3.4% defect rate and quote for lower-carbon blocks. This uses existing staff, gives immediate objections and answers, and directly targets the 61% who would pay up to $0.30 more. It is slower to scale and consumes scarce management time while labour turnover is rising.

Recommendation: TBK should choose direct meetings with housebuilders, supported by a small trade-journal notice. Direct meetings convert the 61% willing to pay a premium and let TBK prove its recycled content to the 44% who check it. National advertising is rejected as costly and geographically wasteful; association sponsorship is rejected because it lacks the technical detail that tender decisions require.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to TBK.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TBK with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in context with a justified recommendation explaining why journal advertising and sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: TBK's defect rate is 3.4% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for TBK of using its flat structure with democratic leadership to improve operator motivation.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A flat structure reduces layers between Priya and the 48 operators, so staff making chipped blocks can raise problems directly and quickly. Democratic leadership invites their ideas on mould settings, which suits a defect rate of 3.4% that must fall to the 1.5% target. Workers who help design the fix are more likely to own it, lifting quality and protecting the $15.00 selling price and 55,000-unit output.

Point 2: Involvement addresses rising labour turnover because operators feel valued rather than directed, improving retention on the automated moulds where skills are scarce. Keeping experienced staff reduces the need to train replacements and helps the $560,000 moulding line reach full output smoothly. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year, stable, motivated employees also limit the disruption and recruitment expense that high turnover would otherwise create during the expansion.

Priya should also remember that democratic leadership takes time and can slow decisions when the 3.4% defect rate needs immediate action; a flat structure works best if operators are trained to use their voice responsibly, so the $640 certification budget and the 1.5% target should be communicated clearly alongside the new authority.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of flat/democratic structures (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to TBK's defects, turnover, output and expansion.

questions.question_text: TBK must train 14 mould operators. Consider certified courses at the local college at $640 per person or on-the-job coaching on the line. Which should TBK choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Certified college courses at $640 per person: A recognised qualification gives the 14 operators structured knowledge of automated moulding and an external standard to meet, valuable when the defect rate is 3.4% against a 1.5% target. The direct cost is $640 x 14 = $8,960, modest beside the $560,000 investment. Drawbacks are that staff are away from the line, reducing short-term output, and generic college content may not match TBK's exact mould settings.

On-the-job coaching: Coaching at the moulding line is machine-specific, costs no fees and keeps all 14 operators productive, protecting output of 55,000 blocks. Experienced operators can demonstrate the recycled-aggregate mixing routine immediately. However, bad habits can be passed on, there is no formal certificate to show housebuilders, and with labour turnover rising the investment may be lost if trainees leave.

Decision: TBK should choose certified college courses followed by short on-site coaching. The certificate helps drive defects from 4.9% toward the 1.5% target and reassures the 44% of builders checking recycled content; $8,960 is small beside $560,000. On-the-job coaching alone is rejected because it offers no external proof of competence and is weakened by rising labour turnover.

Beyond cost, TBK should weigh the 3.4% defect problem: certified operators are more likely to hit the 1.5% target, reducing the 31 monthly complaints and protecting the $15.00 price. With 48 staff and rising turnover, the $8,960 fee is easier to justify if it improves retention, whereas coaching alone may leave the moulding line dependent on a few experienced workers who might leave.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TBK.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of TBK.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, certification and turnover, rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TBK's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety against 55,000-unit output; premium-pricing analysis against $280,000 fixed costs; loan-service targets for the $560,000 line; and unit-cost benchmarking at $13.09 to attack defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $280,000 / ($15.00 - $8.00) = $280,000 / $7.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.00 - $8.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TBK's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 40,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 55,000 units gives a margin of safety of 15,000 units, showing the headroom before the $560,000 moulding line makes a loss.
2. Contribution of $7.00 lets managers test the $0.30 premium surveyed builders accept: at $15.30 price, contribution rises to $7.30, quantifying the benefit of the lower-carbon positioning.
3. With $280,000 fixed costs and $7.00 contribution, managers can set the volume needed to service the $200,000 bank loan before expanding further.
4. Average total cost of $280,000 / 55,000 + $8.00 is about $13.09 a unit; tracking this helps detect the cost of the 3.4% defect rate and the extra mixing time from recycled aggregate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TBK's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has TBK's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $1,750,000 on revenue of $5,000,000 gives 35.0% in 2024; $2,400,000 on $6,000,000 gives 40.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $500,000 on $5,000,000 revenue is 10.0%, and $720,000 on $6,000,000 is 12.0% in 2025. Returns on the capital base are $500,000 / $3,125,000 = 16.0% and $720,000 / $3,600,000 = 20.0%.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The gross margin rose from 35.0% to 40.0%, so a smaller share of the growing $6,000,000 revenue was absorbed by cost of sales, consistent with the 2.8% waste reduction from recycled aggregate. Operating margin improved from 10.0% to 12.0%, meaning operating profit grew faster than revenue despite the 3.4% defect problem. The return on capital increased from 16.0% to 20.0%, so the extra $475,000 of capital employed generated a better return. The operating margin is the stronger evidence because it shows the underlying trading result after operating costs, which is what the new moulding line must improve; the gross margin alone could rise simply because input prices fell. Interest payable edged up only from $35,000 to $45,000, so financing costs are not driving the change.

Conclusion: TBK's financial performance has improved. The three measures moved together in a favourable direction, and the rise in returns is the result of higher profit rather than a smaller capital base.

The modest rise in interest payable from $35,000 to $45,000 shows the improvement is operating rather than financing-led.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of margins and capital use and a justified conclusion, naming the stronger evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TBK of using recycled aggregate in its blocks.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled aggregate cut raw-material waste by 2.8% in the trial and supports the lower-carbon story that 61% of surveyed builders will pay up to $0.30 more for. It protects the $15.00 selling price and the 55,000-unit output from the $560,000 moulding line, and helps satisfy the 44% of housebuilders who check recycled content when tendering, strengthening TBK's position in a competitive regional market.

Disadvantage: The trial raised mixing time by 1.2 minutes per batch, which increases labour and energy use and could push the $8.00 variable cost per unit up, squeezing the $7.00 contribution. Recycled feedstock can also vary in quality, so it may worsen the 3.4% defect rate and the complaints about chipped blocks unless inspection is tightened. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year, any slowdown threatens the margin of safety over the 40,000-unit break-even output.

Priya should set the 2.8% waste saving against the extra 1.2 minutes of mixing time and the $640 training cost before judging the net benefit to the 1.5% defect target.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TBK's trial data, survey and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in cement, steel and recycled-aggregate input costs will affect TBK. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If TBK's $200,000 expansion loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $200,000 = $1,500 a year, small next to $280,000 fixed costs. A fixed-rate loan removes the immediate effect, though future borrowing for the $560,000 line could cost more and higher rates may slow housebuilding.

Minimum wage rise (6.2%, to $12.96 per hour): TBK has a workforce of 48 in moulding and packing roles largely paid hourly, so wage bills rise and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours or individual pay, so no honest annual wage total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity, 55,000 units / 48 staff being about 1,146 blocks per worker. If that holds, the rise is manageable; if rising labour turnover cuts it, unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution shrinks.

Input cost inflation (11.3% on cement, steel and recycled aggregate): The insert does not decompose the $8.00 variable cost, so only a bounded computation is shown: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3%, that adds 11.3% x $8.00 = $0.904, about $0.90 a unit; at 55,000 units that is $49,700 a year. Contribution would fall from $7.00 toward $6.10.

Conclusion: The 11.3% input-cost rise has the greatest impact. It hits every block produced, directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that funds the $560,000 line and cannot be neutralised by fixing a loan rate. The interest rise is at most $1,500 and the wage rise can be offset by productivity; neither touches every unit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TBK.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on TBK's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a justified greatest-impact judgement rejecting the other two.
